Taking Wuhan as the study context, this work proposes an AI-driven framework for public-building energy prediction that integrates multi-building agent-based modeling (MABM), building information modeling (BIM), and deep learning (DL) to forecast energy use in hospitals, shopping malls and office buildings. An MABM-BIM model is first developed and then calibrated and validated against one year of measured data from the three building types. The model explicitly represents the coupled processes among indoor layout, occupant behavior and energy use, and generates synthetic energy time series that are both behaviorally plausible and consistent with widely used calibration criteria. On this basis, four deep learning predictors (DNN, RNN, LSTM and Transformer) are trained on a combination of simulated and measured data and are benchmarked against a representative baseline model from the literature. Across the three building types, the proposed AI models increase R2 by 12.9%–14.0% and Accuracy by 12.2%–13.0%, while reducing MSE, MAE and MAAPE. The Transformer delivers the best overall performance, highlighting the advantage of attention-based architectures for learning long-horizon temporal dependencies and cross-feature interactions. The trained predictors can be embedded as BIM-linked modules to support rapid energy estimation in planning and conceptual design, thus enabling data-driven scheme screening and sustainability-oriented decision-making for public buildings in hot-summer and cold-winter climatic regions.

title: Attributing the urban heat island effect to urban land use patterns with integrated machine learning and GeoShapley method
abstract: Urban land-use patterns are fundamentally associated with the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect. However, conventional models struggle to capture the complex non-linear associations and spatial heterogeneity between land layouts and Land Surface Temperature (LST). This study characterizes these associations using high-resolution land-use data and a spatially interpretable framework integrating machine learning with the GeoShapley method. To ensure methodological robustness, a Spatial Block Cross-Validation (SBCV) strategy was implemented. Layout features were quantified across four dimensions: coverage, connectivity, complexity, and aggregation. Key findings indicate:(1) After decoupling the background thermal effects of geographic location, green space and agricultural land are identified as the optimal land types for heat mitigation, while industrial land is the primary contributor to UHI intensification. In terms of land layout, coverage and connectivity exert significantly greater influence on the thermal environment than aggregation and complexity. (2) Residential and green space coverage exhibit monotonic associations with the UHI effect. In contrast, agricultural and industrial coverage demonstrate pronounced threshold effects, where their impacts stabilize after reaching specific levels.(3) The UHI attribution of land use displays significant spatial heterogeneity, most prominently in green space coverage, whose cooling efficiency is notably attenuated in high-density built-up areas.(4) The impacts of different land-use combinations on the UHI effect vary significantly, with some combinations generating synergistic effects while others exhibit spatial substitution. By identifying dominant land types and sensitive layout intervals, this study deepens the understanding of urban climate mechanisms and provides a scientific basis for formulating precise thermal environment management strategies.

title: Unraveling the coupling-driven patterns of urban carbon emissions and urban heat islands: An LCZ-based interpretable machine learning approach
abstract: The coupling of Urban Carbon Emissions (UCE) and Urban Heat Islands (UHI) poses a critical challenge to sustainable urban development. While their static correlation is widely recognized, the mechanisms underlying their dynamic synchrony remain poorly understood. Furthermore, traditional urban morphological indicators are often limited in identifying priority intervention areas and may fail to capture the heterogeneity driven by diverse climatic and economic backgrounds. To address this, this study adopted the Local Climate Zone (LCZ) framework as a standardized physical descriptor to unravel UCE–UHI coupling patterns. Based on data from 2714 counties in China, we developed an XGBoost-TPE model combined with SHAP to facilitate mechanistic insights. Our key findings were as follows: (1) UCE and UHI in Chinese counties from 2015 to 2021 exhibited a significant global positive correlation (Moran’s I: 0.203–0.212, p-value < 0.01), but showed asynchronous dynamic changes in the northwest and western regions. (2) The LCZ-based model demonstrated high predictive consistency across all clusters (R2 of cross-validation > 0.85). (3) The key drivers of UCE and UHI exhibited heterogeneity: built-type LCZs appeared to be more critical for UCE, while natural-type LCZs tended to exert a more pronounced influence on UHI. (4) LCZs’ effects varied significantly with climatic backgrounds, with different directions, magnitudes, and transition thresholds (LCZs 2–3: 0.2%–6.9%, LCZs 4–6: 1.3%–20.5%, LCZs 7–10: 0.8%–13.9%, LCZs E-F: 1.2%–1.3%). (5) Synergistic, antagonistic, and complex phase-based compound interactions between LCZs were identified. By linking urban morphological characteristics with environmental responses, this study highlights the analytical potential of the LCZ framework for diagnosing UCE–UHI coupling dynamics. The results provide a quantitative, evidence-informed basis to support context-sensitive urban planning and targeted mitigation strategies.

title: Unraveling the impacts of multidimensional urban influencing factors on daytime and nighttime thermal environments across urban functional zones using SDGSAT-1 data and XGBoost-GeoShapley analysis
abstract: Although numerous researches have explored how urban influencing factors influences land surface temperature (LST), comparatively limited attention has been given to analyses based on urban functional zones (UFZs), especially those that investigate and contrast the driving mechanisms between daytime and nighttime conditions. Furthermore, numerous studies have analyzed this driving mechanism using interpretable machine learning methods that typically rely on the standard SHAP framework, yet this approach overlooks the inherent spatial dependency. In our study, high-resolution daytime and nighttime thermal infrared data from SDGSAT-1 were integrated with multi-source urban datasets for Fuzhou, China. An interpretable integrated XGBoost-GeoShapley framework was applied to comprehensively investigate the determinants of LST during summer daytime and nighttime among six predominant UFZs. The results reveal a fundamental daytime and nighttime shift in thermal drivers: built-environment indices dictate daytime sensible heat accumulation, whereas ecological factors dominate nocturnal latent heat cooling. Simultaneously building density acts as a severe daytime warmer but transitions to a relative nocturnal cooler in dense commercial cores due to the urban canyon mutual shading effect. Furthermore, ecological cooling demonstrates a biological threshold. Crucially, GeoShapley analysis uncovers that spatial interaction effects are substantially stronger at night, accounting for 38.2% of the integrated zone, with residential zones reaching 33.6%. This research establishes a spatially explicit analytical framework to unravel the multifactorial influences shaping the urban thermal environment and delivers scientific evidence that supports the development of spatially and temporally adaptive strategies for urban heat mitigation and planning.

title: Enhancing thermal resilience of heat–cold island networks in lake-ring urban agglomerations using machine learning and multi-scenario simulations
abstract: Under rapid urbanization and climate warming, urban heat island (UHI) effects in lake-ring urban agglomerations have intensified. Prior studies often emphasize single patches or local scales, obscuring regional heat–cold connectivity and limiting network-based resilience planning under future scenarios. This study integrates morphological spatial pattern analysis (MSPA) with circuit theory to construct a heat–cold island (HCI) composite network comprising sources, corridors, and nodes. In this framework, machine learning characterizes nonlinear thermal-connectivity resistance, while the patch-generating land-use simulation (PLUS) model simulates HCI network reorganization under multiple 2030 scenarios. A land surface temperature (LST)-derived surface thermal structural resilience framework was then developed to link historical and future network changes. Evidence from the Taihu Lake urban agglomeration indicates that from 2000 to 2020, heat island (HI) sources expanded rapidly across the eastern lakeside built-up area, with marked increases in corridors and nodes. In contrast, cold island (CI) networks became increasingly fragmented. HCI composite nodes shifted from the Taihu Lake shoreline toward the western ecological transition zone. By 2030, SSP585 formed a strong heat-connectivity network, and cooling connectivity pathways were nearly lost. Under SSP119, barriers to cold-source connectivity were reduced, and CI corridors increased. The surface thermal structural resilience improvement index (TR) showed strong structural dependence, remaining negative historically and declining further under SSP245 and SSP585. By contrast, SSP119 increased TR to −0.134 through cooling-corridor recovery and key-node reorganization, approaching a more balanced network structure. This study reframes LST-based surface thermal structural resilience from a whole-network HCI perspective and provides guidance for climate-adaptive spatial planning.

title: Data-driven risk assessment of climate-related failures in railway infrastructure
abstract: Climate-related failures pose increasing risks to railway operation and maintenance, requiring robust assessments to support effective resilience planning. Accordingly, this study presents a comprehensive risk assessment to identify, quantify, and prioritize climate-related failure modes (CRFMs). CRFMs were identified through text mining of 15-year corrective maintenance records across all five Swedish railway regions. A probabilistic model was then developed to analyze the risk of identified CRFMs, considering both operational and maintenance costs. Risk distributions were derived using Monte Carlo simulation and summarized by Expected Value of Risk (EVoR) and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR 0.90 ). As a result, 14 CRFMs were identified, accounting for 47% of all failure records. Their annual trend and seasonal distribution align well with periods of increased extreme weather events and dominant seasonal climate hazards. Furthermore, clustering the regional profile of CRFMs reveals regional similarity. The CRFMs were then prioritized, showing that 4 modes (i.e., Track deformation, Snow and ice, Buckling, and Rail breakage/crack) account for 73% of total CVaR 0.90 . The amplification of total risk in the tail indicates a 74% higher cost burden under extreme conditions. Finally, regional climate vulnerability was assessed using risk metrics normalized by track length and traffic density.

title: Deciphering the impacts of urban gray–green spaces on seasonal diurnal land surface temperature in a valley-basin city via explainable machine learning
abstract: The Urban Heat Island effect poses a major challenge to sustainable development, and understanding its driving factors is crucial for improving the urban thermal environment. The nonlinear effects of urban gray–green spaces on Land Surface Temperature (LST) under valley-basin conditions remain systematically underexplored. This study investigates Changsha, a typical valley-basin city, by integrating Morphological Spatial Pattern Analysis with landscape metrics to construct a comprehensive gray–green spaces framework. Using explainable machine learning (CatBoost-SHAP), we quantify the nonlinear and interactive effects of eight composite indicators on seasonal diurnal LST. Results show: (1) Gray space indicators contribute 51.6–59.2% to daytime LST across spring, summer, and winter, with BMSF as the dominant positive driver; green space indicators contribute 57.5–65.2% to nighttime LST, led by GACI and GMSF. (2) Threshold effects are evident: BMSF warming saturates beyond +0.5 SD, while GCI cooling diminishes after +0.5 SD, with marginal returns dropping from 0.25 °C per unit to near zero. GACI shows a unique positive effect (+0.3 °C) on winter nights. (3) Interactions reveal synergistic heating (BMSF×BCI > 0.25 SHAP), synergistic cooling (GMSF×GCI <−0.4 SHAP), and asymmetric buffering where high GMSF reduces BMSF thermal load by up to 0.6 SHAP. This study underscores gray–green interplay as a key driver of urban thermal dynamics in valley-basin cities, revealing quantifiable nonlinear balances. Based on these findings, we propose a regulatory strategy integrating spatiotemporal control, synergistic optimization, and topographic adaptation.

title: Identifying CO2 emission reduction strategies tailored to different building types by integrating multi-scale factors via deep learning
abstract: Reducing carbon emissions in the building sector is a critical challenge for urban decarbonization. Buildings differ substantially in their functions, usage intensities, and operational characteristics, which require emission reduction strategies tailored to different building types. However, previous studies have been limited in their examination of how building-level characteristics and the surrounding urban environments jointly influence CO2 emissions across different building types. Therefore, this study proposes an artificial intelligence-based analytical framework that integrates building-level characteristics with urban environmental factors to assess their effects on CO2 emissions across different building types. This framework captures non-linear relationships between the multi-scale factors and CO2 emissions and assesses their effects using model interpretation techniques, simulating changes from current states. The findings of this study indicate that increasing floor area ratio (FAR) generally reduces CO2 emissions, whereas emissions increase in public buildings when the FAR is increased by 140% relative to its current level. Increasing south-facing building surface area showed the potential to substantially reduce emissions in low-rise residential and public buildings. Furthermore, the increased green area ratio (GAR) effectively mitigated emissions in residential buildings, while exhibiting a rebound effect in commercial buildings when increased by 12%. These findings highlight the importance of building-type-specific and threshold-based strategies for effective urban building decarbonization. Moreover, this framework provides quantitative evidence for developing building-type-specific regulatory standards and design guidelines, supporting more targeted and effective urban building decarbonization.

title: A comparative assessment of sampling strategies for tree-based machine learning models in urban flood susceptibility prediction with imbalanced data
abstract: Flood susceptibility mapping identifies flood-prone areas, providing scientific support for flood prevention planning and resilient infrastructure. However, the accuracy of machine learning models in flood susceptibility mapping is compromised by imbalanced data. Moreover, systematic comparative assessments of sampling strategies for tree-based models in urban flood susceptibility prediction are lacking, and the intricate nonlinear correlations between flood susceptibility and its underlying drivers remain insufficiently explored. This study developed a novel framework that systematically investigates the effect of sampling methods and non-flooding samples ratios on tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM) in urban flood susceptibility prediction in Beijing, China, and places a dual emphasis on predictive performance and model interpretability via Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) analyses to interpret the key drivers. Results show that models using one-class support vector machine (OC SVM) method (Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) ≥ 0.92) consistently outperformed those using random sampling at 1:3 and 1:5 ratios. Specifically, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model with OC SVM at a 1:3 ratio attained the highest AUC value (0.938) and Geometric Mean (G-mean) (0.845) across all sampling methods and ratios, and exhibited a more balanced and rational spatial pattern in flood susceptibility prediction. The top four factors contributing to flood susceptibility were Gross Domestic Product (GDP) level (28.04%), mean building height (15.96%), distance to roads (15.31%), and Digital Elevation Model (DEM) (9.67%). PDP analysis revealed urban flood susceptibility initially increases significantly with GDP, and then declines and stabilizes after a critical point. A strong near-linear positive relationship was evident between building height and flood susceptibility. Flood susceptibility significantly decreases as distance to roads increased and eventually stabilizes. This study provides empirical evidence and methodological guidance for selecting sampling strategies in applying machine learning models for urban flood susceptibility prediction.

title: Toward interpretable urban spatial layout generation: Encoding domain knowledge into graph neural networks
abstract: While deep neural networks advance urban spatial layout (USL) generation, the uninterpretable nature restricts their practical application in human-value-aligned planning scenarios. This study presents the Hierarchical Causal Graph Neural Network with Domain Knowledge Constraints (HCGNN-DKC). This is a neuro-symbolic model that internalises the ontology and expert priors from the planning domain into the information delivery mechanism, while further regularising the model’s predictive scope through logical rules. Evaluations indicate that HCGNN-DKC significantly outperforms baseline models in performance (average accuracy of 85.2%, recall of 74.1%, MSE of 0.523) and generalisability. Crucially, rule-violation test results and real-world applications prove that the embedded logical rules serve as a safety guardrail, effectively mitigating physical violations. Furthermore, whilst adhering to prior knowledge, the model exhibits an autonomous knowledge discovery capability that transcends expert presets. The semantic proximity shown by our framework provides a vital bridge between planning semantics and spatial modelling, establishing an interpretable and intelligent knowledge-based planning support systems.

title: Automated urban energy assessment: From thermal flyover to AI-driven retrofit prioritization for sustainable cities
abstract: Cities urgently need scalable methods to assess building energy performance for retrofit prioritization, yet current approaches are costly and slow for comprehensive urban energy planning. We present an automated pipeline that transforms thermal flyovers into actionable energy assessments using AI-driven analysis. Our approach segments mid-wave infrared orthomosaics into building patches using an unsupervised multi-modal pipeline (Thermal-SAM), extracts physically interpretable ring and context features, and benchmarks energy-use intensity (EUI) derived from aggregated EPC records. We exclude implausible EUI records above 1000 kWh/m2/yr from primary model-performance evaluation. On this screened dataset (n=1190), leakage-free non-thermal covariates achieve RMSE = 26.84 and MAE = 16.13 kWh/m2/yr, within the range reported by recent EPC-based prediction studies. An EPC-full upper-bound model that retains energy-consumption proxies achieves lower error (RMSE = 9.36, MAE = 1.31 kWh/m2/yr), but this reflects feature–target proximity rather than independent prediction. Thermal features are therefore not presented as routine direct EUI predictors. Instead, the excluded high-EUI tail is treated as a diagnostic anomaly set: in the unfiltered diagnostic analysis, thermal features help rank the largest thermal–EPC discrepancies (AUC = 0.779, 95% CI 0.774–0.784, 100 seeds), while this signal collapses after the implausible records are removed. These findings reposition thermal flyovers as a scalable tool for triaging buildings with unusually high or inconsistent EPC-derived energy use, while highlighting the limitations of single-pass thermal data for accurate EUI regression. Reproducible code (available upon request) supports rapid, citywide screening and targeted follow-up audits.

title: Causal machine learning uncovers thresholds and seasonal reversal in landscape-meteorology-driven urban Heat-PM₂.₅ coupling
abstract: In the context of rapid urbanization, the mutual amplification between the urban heat island (UHI) effect and air pollution has emerged as a severe composite environmental challenge. Most existing studies focus on the linear driving mechanisms of individual environmental issues, leaving a systematic understanding of their nonlinear interactions, seasonal dynamics, and causal pathways largely unexplored. To address this gap, this study focuses on the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration in China as a case study. It bridges interpretable machine learning (XGBoost-SHAP) with structural causal modeling (SCM) to systematically quantify the nonlinear impacts and causal mechanisms of blue-green space (BGS) patterns and meteorological factors on land surface temperature (LST) and PM 2.5 concentrations. The results indicate that: (1) LST drivers exhibit a pronounced seasonal shift-BGS coverage dominates in summer, whereas meteorological factors prevail in winter-whereas PM 2.5 is consistently governed by wind speed across seasons; (2) key drivers exhibit threshold effects (e.g., in this study, 40-42% vegetation coverage for LST, 79-80% water aggregation for PM 2.5 ), beyond which they act as “effect-switching thresholds” that reverse the influence of other factors and form a nonlinear interaction network; and (3) SCM reveals the dual causal pathways through which BGS patterns influence the environment-via direct cooling and indirect modulation of wind fields-and quantitatively verifies the stable positive causal effect of PM 2.5 on LST, clarifying the pathway of “pollution exacerbating warming”. In summary, this study uncovers the nonlinear, threshold-dependent characteristics of the UHI-pollution complex system and elucidates their synergistic intensification from a causal perspective, providing a quantitative basis for seasonally adaptive strategies to synergistically mitigate urban heat and pollution.

title: Enhancing interdependent infrastructure systems resilience in post-disaster recovery: A social-technical approach based on reinforcement learning
abstract: A social-technical approach integrating the Infrastructure Hetero-functional Graph (IHFG) and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is proposed for the collaborative recovery of post-disaster multi-infrastructure systems. A "physical entity–functional node–service process" mapping mechanism is established to explicitly characterize complex system interdependencies. Furthermore, a reward mechanism driven by hierarchical resident needs is integrated to facilitate service-oriented recovery within highly dynamic and complex environments. In a case study of a coupled transportation-power-gas-water network in Jingdezhen, optimal repair strategies under multi-hazard scenarios were explored. The results show that IHFG-MARL with dynamic weights can generate system-level recovery strategies that account for complex interdependencies and achieve relatively robust resilience improvement under different disaster conditions. In rainfall-driven scenarios, the proposed method and the genetic algorithm both show strong performance, whereas the advantage of IHFG-MARL with dynamic weights becomes more evident under the full-damage stress-test scenario. This indicates that the proposed method has stronger strategic adaptability in complex interdependent networks and under high-intensity disturbances. In addition, the embedded dynamic demand mechanism enables the recovery process to prioritize residents’ basic survival needs and gradually shift toward broader functional service needs as recovery progresses, thereby forming recovery pathways consistent with the hierarchical evolution of residents’ needs.

title: Urban airflow field prediction using sparse sensors: A hybrid data-driven approach with reduced-order modeling
abstract: Urban airflow field modeling can provide cities with monitoring solutions to enhance pedestrian/cyclists comfort, improve air quality, and enhance urban wind energy generation yield. In addition, it could support a safe and efficient deployment of urban air mobility (UAM) supporting the next generation of faster and more sustainable means of urban transport reducing the congestion and traffic. However, real-time wind monitoring across urban areas remains a significant challenge due to spatial and temporal variations and uncertainties. This study presents an integrated framework that serves as a surrogate model for the real-time reconstruction and prediction of wind velocity fields around a simplified urban building configuration. The approach relies exclusively on online sensor measurements and employs reduced-order modeling techniques for dimensionality reduction, thereby improving computational efficiency. The offline development of the model integrates three principal components: (1) a bidirectional long short-term memory (BILSTM) network trained on airflow sensor data to capture temporal dynamics, (2) a sparsity-promoting dynamic mode decomposition (SP-DMD) for extracting dominant spatial modes of airflow, and (3) a multi-task learning (MTL) network to map sensor signals. The proposed framework was assessed against high-fidelity CFD simulations of wind flow around a high-rise urban building. The results indicate that the proposed three-stage method reliably reconstructs accurate urban airflow fields in real time under varying levels of sensor noise, and demonstrate its feasibility for sparse-sensor reconstruction under the tested sensor-placement configurations. Moreover, these findings demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly reduce operational/computational costs and shows strong potential as a surrogate tool for next-generation of urban airflow monitoring.

title: Revealing the diurnal drivers of land surface temperature using artificial neural network models: A case study in Changsha-Zhuzhou-Xiangtan metropolitan area, China
abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified the urban heat island (UHI) effect, highlighting the need to better understand the factors associated with land surface temperature (LST) in order to improve local thermal environments. Although previous studies have shown that urbanization and environmental conditions can significantly influence LST, their relative importance, nonlinear relationships, and differences between daytime and nighttime remain insufficiently understood. The Changsha-Zhuzhou-Xiangtan (CZT) metropolitan area, one of China’s first national pilot zones for building a resource-efficient and environment-friendly society, is a representative metropolitan region characterized by a compact polycentric structure and pronounced natural-urban spatial heterogeneity. Using artificial neural network models and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), this study identifies the relative importance and nonlinear associations of multiple spatial and environmental factors with daytime and nighttime LST. This analysis is data-driven, and the physical mechanisms discussed in this study are intended only as plausible interpretations of the observed patterns rather than as directly tested processes. The results show that: (1) Elevation had the strongest association with both daytime and nighttime LST, followed by indicators of human activity intensity; (2) water bodies and densely vegetated areas exhibited clear cooling effects during the daytime, whereas water bodies showed relatively higher LST at night, shifting from daytime cold spots to nighttime hot spots; (3) all factors exhibited nonlinear associations with LST, and marginal effect curves revealed critical ranges and inflection points for daytime and nighttime LST variations; and (4) nonlinear statistical approaches are useful for quantitatively characterizing the complex relationships between LST and multiple spatial-environmental factors at the metropolitan scale. These findings provide refined and differentiated decision support for urban heat mitigation and spatial planning.

title: Prioritizing ‘greenable areas’ for urban heat relief by integrating heat risk, cooling potential, and welfare equity: A data-driven framework with a case study of Nanjing, China
abstract: Urban heat risk is intensifying in compact, high-density cities where opportunities for new green space are limited. Existing prioritization studies often identify where cooling is needed, but less often ask whether greening is feasible or where it would yield the largest marginal benefit. This study introduces greenable areas, defined as residual urban spaces that can be converted to vegetation within dense built-up fabrics. We develop a decision-support workflow that identifies these spaces, assesses heat risk, predicts scenario-based LST cooling with a machine-learning model, and estimates welfare gains in population-weighted green-space accessibility, with all outputs aggregated to street blocks. A case study in the main urban area of Nanjing, China shows how the framework can produce priority maps for feasible infill greening under limited land resources. By linking need, feasibility, cooling potential, and welfare equity, the study provides a replicable screening approach for urban heat adaptation in space-constrained environments.

title: Impact of natural and artificial cover on LST in cities, with a focus on comparison of single- and multi-ring buffers
abstract: Land surface temperature (LST) is a representative indicator for predicting urban heat island. The single-buffer approach, which has been used to analyze the relationship between LST and explanatory variables, cannot capture the effects of both the distance of independent variables and the area of land cover included within the buffer zone. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the relationship between LST and natural and artificial land cover in urban regions, using a multi-ring buffer model to refine independent variables in 50-m increments, by land cover type. Four tree-based machine learning models—Random Forest, LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost—were compared. XGBoost exhibited the highest performance, with R² range of 0.88–0.98 across 50–500-m intervals. LST prediction analysis was effective up to 350 m. Further, the significant spatial range of variables shifted with 50-m intervals, enabling a more granular analysis of the significant spatial range of independent variables. The restoration simulation showed that greening efforts on the Western Arterial Road and Jemulpo Tunnel reduced LST within an approximate range of 150 m. These findings provide crucial scientific evidence for determining the placement of urban parks and formulating urban planning and management strategies aimed at optimizing LST reduction in urban environments.

title: Strategic and equitable allocation of electric vehicle fast charging stations using geospatial-aware multi-objective deep reinforcement learning
abstract: Public fast charging infrastructure is becoming an essential component of sustainable urban mobility as cities transition toward low-carbon transportation (e.g., Electric Vehicles (EVs)). However, suboptimal deployment can exacerbate spatial disparities in service accessibility, limit the practical benefits of EV adoption, and create localized stress on urban distribution grids. Despite recent advances in the allocation and placement of electric vehicle fast charging stations (FCSs), existing decision-support approaches remain limited in their ability to coordinate multiple objectives across large, spatially heterogeneous urban systems. This study thus proposes a multi-objective sequential decision-making model for the placement and sizing of FCS, integrated with solar power supply, across large and complex urban environments. By integrating a federated learning-based multi-objective deep reinforcement learning (FLMODRL) framework with geospatial analysis, the proposed model identifies EVFCS sites through a global policy that aggregates locally learned policies to achieve balanced performance across environmental, economic, and urbanity objectives. The proposed FLMORL model shows it capability to determine both the optimal placement and capacity of FCS by outperforming single-agent weight-summed reward scalarization deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Specifically, the model identifies 520 fast charging stations in Chicago that exceed a high reward threshold (e.g., >10), indicating locations that simultaneously satisfy all objectives. In addition, the proposed deployment scenario suggests the potential of the learned spatial allocation strategy to improve population-weighted accessibility across income groups in Chicago. Overall, the results demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in supporting strategic and accessibility-aware FCS allocation across the urban area, contributing to more sustainable and resilient charging infrastructure planning.
keywords: Allocation and placement of charging stations

title: From physical surfaces to human-centric heat stress: LST and UTCI heat mapping reveals nonlinear effects of urban morphology
abstract: Heat exposure connects the built environment and public health, directly shaping the livability and sustainability of urban areas. Fully understanding the spatial heterogeneity of heat exposure and its driving factors is therefore a vital prerequisite for climate-adaptive urban planning. However, most planning-oriented studies rely on land surface temperature (LST), and whether LST adequately represents human heat exposure and how it differs from physiologically relevant heat stress remains insufficiently examined. Here, adopting Landsat-retrieved 30-m LST and GPU-accelerated 1-m universal thermal climate index (UTCI) in Singapore, this study establishes a comprehensive “Modeling-Comparing-Assessing” framework to systematically evaluate the spatial and mechanistic discrepancies between the two metrics. We further investigate pronounced non-stationary and threshold-based quantitative relationships of the two metrics with urban factors by employing a novel geographically weighted XGBoost (GW-XGBoost) and generalized additive model (GAM) workflow. Our results demonstrate notable discrepancies in spatial patterns of LST and UTCI, along with substantial spatial heterogeneity in how 2D and 3D urban factors impact these two thermal metrics, as revealed by explainable GW-XGBoost models (the test R 2 = 0.855 for LST and 0.905 for UTCI, respectively). Crucially, spatially explicit SHAP interprets that sky view factor plays a central role in explaining UTCI variability but exhibits a comparatively marginal independent contribution to LST, indicating that LST inadequately captures shading-driven and radiative processes governing actual human heat stress. Notably, SHAP-GAM analysis indicates that higher albedo is associated with increased UTCI. These novel findings provide model-informed planning implications for integrating physiologically relevant thermal indices to support targeted heat risk management and climate-adaptive urban planning.

title: Nonlinear driving mechanisms of land surface temperature under the coupling of blue-green space and urbanization: An analysis based on explainable machine learning
abstract: Urban thermal stress has intensified under climate change and rapid urbanization. Blue-green space (BGS) is a key form of ecological infrastructure for mitigating urban heat; however, its thermal effects are jointly shaped by landscape patterns, urbanization intensity, and development-stage differences. Using Zhengzhou, China, as a case study, this study integrated blue-green space–urbanization coupling with interpretable land surface temperature (LST) modelling by combining coupling coordination degree (CCD) classification, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) attribution, robustness tests, and breakpoint validation. The results showed that CCD increased continuously from 2003 to 2023 and exhibited a clustered spatial pattern, with higher values in the urban core and lower values in the suburban fringe. The dominant drivers of LST varied across CCD gradients. In the low-coordination gradient, the primary model-attributed driver shifted from built-up percentage (BP) to forest percentage (FP), whereas in the middle- and higher-coordination gradients, water percentage (WP) and population density (POP) generally showed stronger contributions to model predictions. Nonlinear response analysis indicated that the effects of key blue-green-space and urbanization indicators were stage-dependent rather than governed by fixed thresholds. Fractional vegetation cover (FVC) exhibited the most consistent model-derived response interval, with nonlinear changes concentrated around 0.55–0.63 in the middle and later periods. BP showed later-stage warming-related warning intervals, mainly around 0.79–0.81, in middle- and higher-coordination gradients. WP showed weaker temporal stability, with a case-specific response interval around 0.17 observed mainly in the 2023 higher-coordination gradient. These findings provide case-based, model-derived evidence for differentiated heat-mitigation strategies in Zhengzhou and offer a methodological reference for testing similar coupled urban systems elsewhere.

title: Assessing urban waterlogging risk and nonlinear drivers in high density cities: A multi model machine learning comparative approach
abstract: Under the combined pressures of climate change and rapid urbanization, high density cities are facing increasing risks of urban waterlogging (UW) during extreme rainfall events. However, existing UW risk assessments often lack systematic comparisons of different machine learning models and provide limited insight into nonlinear driving mechanisms. Taking Shenzhen, a representative high density city in China, as a case study, this research develops an integrated assessment framework that combines multi source spatial data, multi model machine learning comparison, and explainable artificial intelligence techniques. Thirteen risk factors are selected from the perspectives of hazard, environmental susceptibility, and exposure. Four ensemble tree-based models, namely Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Decision Tree, Extreme Gradient Boosting, and Light Gradient Boosting Machine, are applied and compared for UW risk prediction. The results show that the RF model achieves the best overall performance, with high-risk areas identified by the model covering 92.45% of historical UW locations. Spatially, UW risk in Shenzhen exhibits a pronounced southeast low and northwest high pattern, closely associated with highly urbanized and densely populated areas. Model SHAP and PDP analyses further reveal strong nonlinear and threshold effects among key risk factors. Impervious surface area, population density, and GDP are identified as the most influential factors associated with UW risk. In particular, road density shows a pronounced U-shaped relationship with UW risk, highlighting the dual role of road systems in drainage organization and impervious surface expansion. Overall, this study provides a transferable framework for resilience governance and spatial optimization in high density cities.

title: Where could urban tree canopy expansion lower modeled summer cooling-energy demand? An equity-informed explainable machine-learning framework for Washington, DC
abstract: Urban heat and rising summer cooling demand are increasingly important equity concerns in U.S. cities, yet fine-scale evidence on where urban greening may reduce summer cooling-energy demand remains limited. This study examines modeled summer cooling-energy demand across Census Block Groups (CBGs) in Washington, DC, with emphasis on the environmental and social conditions shaping neighborhood-scale cooling demand and the potential role of targeted tree-canopy expansion. We integrate indicators of tree canopy, imperviousness, planting opportunity, and neighborhood deprivation. Using spatially cross-validated XGBoost with a monotonic canopy constraint, SHAP-based interpretation, threshold identification, and counterfactual canopy scenarios, we identify where canopy intervention is most likely to provide benefit. Results show that modeled cooling demand is spatially concentrated in Wards 7 and 8, where higher deprivation, lower canopy, and less favorable built-environment conditions coincide. In contrast, Ward 3 exhibits the lowest deprivation, highest canopy, and lowest modeled cooling demand. Imperviousness alone does not fully explain modeled cooling demand: some areas show high imperviousness but relatively lower demand, suggesting that housing quality and broader socioeconomic advantage may condition the energy consequences of heat exposure. Areas with lower tree canopy tended to exhibit higher modeled cooling-energy demand, although this pattern varied with surrounding environmental and built-environment conditions. A model-derived canopy screening benchmark of approximately 21% in Wards 7 and 8 suggests that the strongest modeled cooling benefits are likely to occur in low-canopy neighborhoods below this benchmark. In both wards, about 64% of CBGs fell below the threshold. Planting opportunity emerges as the strongest implementation-relevant predictor. Overall, the findings provide an equity-centered framework for targeting urban greening to reduce modeled cooling-energy demand and support climate adaptation.

title: SHAP-TAG: Operationalizing explainable AI for urban heat governance through attribution-severity typologies and policy triggers
abstract: Urban heat adaptation increasingly relies on spatially explicit diagnostics, yet explainable AI outputs often remain difficult to translate into planning decisions. This study introduces SHAP-TAG (SHAP-based Typology and Actionable Governance), a framework that converts grid-level SHAP attributions into governance-ready products: attribution-severity typologies, model-based transition zones, and a tiered policy matrix. Using 30-m summer daytime land surface temperature (LST) modeling for the Greater Taipei Metropolitan Area, we distinguish a global diagnostic model from an urban action model to reduce topographic masking and focus interpretation on governance-facing built-environment drivers. The urban action model achieved a spatial cross-validation R² of 0.540 and MAE of 1.85°C using nine actionable variables. Compared with the global diagnostic model, NDVI became the dominant governance-facing signal in the urban action model, rising from rank 4 to rank 1 and showing a 2.31-fold increase in mean absolute SHAP magnitude. Full-urban SHAP clustering identified four attribution-severity tiers structured primarily by a vegetation-deficit and built-up-intensity gradient, with secondary modulation from openness and surface-composition signals: Strong vegetation–openness cooling core (10.73%), Moderate vegetation-cooling context (18.53%), Near-neutral transitional zone (33.35%), and Vegetation-deficit warming-priority zone (37.39%). These tiers are interpreted as a SHAP-calibrated governance sequence rather than four mutually independent heat mechanisms. NDVI showed a primary SHAP sign-change around 0.275 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.273–0.277), with the operational transition zone spanning approximately 0.27–0.33 when combined with sensitivity-based references. Albedo and sky-view-related indicators exhibited context-dependent attribution patterns and were therefore treated as operational references rather than universal physical thresholds. By linking attribution direction and magnitude, transition zones, and policy tiers, SHAP-TAG provides a locally calibrated but workflow-transferable approach for urban heat governance.

title: Smart point cloud–guided 3D gaussian splatting for urban modeling and data-driven analysis
abstract: This paper proposes a combined Smart Point Cloud (SPC) and Smart 3D Gaussian Splatting (S3DGS) framework for integrated urban analysis at block scale. Using laser-scanning point clouds and multi-view imagery of the aula–library heritage block in Netherlands, we first construct an SPC with CityGML-inspired semantics, then train a 3DGS model from the same image set and project SPC labels onto the Gaussians to obtain an S3DGS representation. On this basis, we derive a family of indicators that are usually produced in separate workflows: façade- and ground-plane composition from semantic projections; panoramic exposure metrics for greenery, buildings and sky from renderings of 3DGS with semantic labels (S3DGS); and column- and voxel-based statistics from the segmented SPC. The results demonstrate that the combined SPC–S3DGS model can simultaneously support plan-based, façade-based and view-dependent indicators, and can distinguish coherent scene types such as highly enclosed façade-adjacent zones, tree-dominated corridors, open plazas and mixed transitional spaces. Reflective surfaces and water, which are poorly captured by laser scanning, are recovered through the image-driven S3DGS component. We argue that SPC–S3DGS provides a generic semantic scene representation that can enrich urban digital twins with a visual–environment layer, and that it offers a promising basis for coupling structural, land-cover and exposure metrics in computational studies of computers, environment and urban systems.

title: Exploring the impacts of logistics space on urban carbon emissions: A hybrid MNL-LightGBM method
abstract: As a major source of urban carbon emissions, logistics space and its interaction with the surrounding environment have become critical to understanding the dynamic patterns of urban carbon emissions. Deeper investigation into how urban logistics land use and facility layouts contribute to the spatial heterogeneity of carbon emissions holds significant implications. Taking the Wuhan Metropolitan Development Area as a case study, this paper proposes the concept of Spatial Environment Induced Carbon-Emission Discrepancy (SEICD), which quantifies emission heterogeneity into carbon mitigation and carbon exacerbation. A hybrid MNL‑LightGBM model is constructed to identify key factors and reveal their nonlinear mechanisms, focusing on the combined effects of logistics facility layout and spatial variables on carbon emissions. Results show that spatial variables, such as industrial land proportion and floor area ratio, exhibit strong nonlinear associations with SEICD. Interactive associations between the number of logistics facilities and distance to small facilities, as well as with FAR and distance to residential land, play particularly prominent roles. Furthermore, grid-scale analysis based on the SHAP method reveals that the layout of large logistics facilities adjacent to industrial land in the urban periphery, as well as areas with high floor area ratio and high land use mix in the central urban area, are conducive to carbon mitigation. By integrating mechanisms across different functional zones, this study constructs an optimization framework and regulatory methods for logistics facility layout based on spatial environmental adaptability, providing quantitative support and planning guidance for the low‑carbon transition of urban logistics systems.

title: A LSTM-EGAN framework for forecasting land surface temperature in urban areas based on time-series datasets
abstract: Land surface temperature (LST) is a key parameter for understanding urban thermal environments and is strongly shaped by both historical and contemporary urban land-use patterns. Jointly considering past land-use trajectories and current planning schemes is therefore essential for understanding the spatio-temporal relationships between urban form and LST, and for anticipating the thermal impacts of future development. This paper proposes a spatio-temporal prediction framework based on a Long Short-Term Memory–Enhanced Generative Adversarial Network (LSTM-EGAN) to generate fine-grained LST predictions from urban planning inputs and historical heat maps. Using Istanbul city as a case study, we train the model on a 10-year historical dataset comprising 1600 paired samples constructed from land-use maps, satellite imagery, and LST products. After quantitative accuracy assessment, we conduct scenario-based simulations to explore planning-relevant principles for urban heat mitigation. In addition, we develop an interactive user interface application for future projects. This study proposes a framework and application with the potential to support data-driven urban planning and design under increasing heat stress.

title: CausalSolar: Leveraging causal representations of residential solar adoption to enhance image-based detection of rooftop solar panels
abstract: Accurate mapping of residential rooftop solar panels is essential for understanding distributed energy transitions. Conventional image-based models often confuse solar panels with visually similar objects, such as skylights or HVAC units, relying solely on visual cues. Conversely, while existing studies identify demographics, building types, and policy as key drivers of solar adoption, these factors are typically used for ex post explanation of past trends rather than a priori prediction. To bridge this gap, this study introduces CausalSolar, a framework that integrates high-resolution visual learning with a Causal Reasoning Module to enhance residential rooftop solar detection and reasoning. Our framework operationalizes adoption mechanisms across domains of People (PE), Place (PL), Neighborhood Effects (NE), and Regional Effects (RE) as active constraints for object detection. Capitalizing on Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), the framework filters out spurious visual correlations and evaluates rooftop candidates based on both appearance and contextual reality. Applied to 428 census tracts across five North Carolina counties (6,419 km²), CausalSolar achieves an F1 score of 92.91%, outperforming state-of-the-art image-only baselines by 7% to 27%. Beyond detection, our framework characterizes the relative contributions of causal factors that shift along the urban-rural gradient: demographic factors (PE) dominate in dense urban cores and peri-urban neighborhoods, while structural, spatial, and policy cues (PL, NE, and RE) drive detection in moderate- to low-density rural neighborhoods. By embedding socio-behavioral evidence into computer vision, CausalSolar provides an accurate and interpretable tool for large-scale renewable energy mapping and sustainable urban planning.

title: Estimating the causal effects of landscape interventions on urban thermal environments using generalized random forests
abstract: A growing wave of urban thermal studies has used machine learning models and post-hoc explanation tools, particularly Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), to rank landscape factors and detect nonlinear thermal responses. Yet such predict-then-explain frameworks are designed to explain fitted models rather than real-world interventions, making them vulnerable to spurious correlations, unstable importance rankings, and ambiguous planning implications. This study applies a causal-diagram-informed generalized random forest (GRF) framework to estimate the effects of landscape interventions on land surface temperature (LST) at the city-block scale in Beijing. Built on adaptive local weighting, GRF constructs randomized-controlled-trial-like comparisons among observationally comparable city blocks, enabling the estimation of unit-specific dose-response intervention effects. The results show that replacing impervious surfaces with water bodies, trees, and croplands significantly reduced LST by 0.050 ± 0.023, 0.042 ± 0.011, and 0.034 ± 0.012 °C per 1% increase, respectively, while increasing building coverage raised LST by 0.022 ± 0.014 °C per 1%. Building height, building-height variability, and surface albedo also generated strong cooling effects, whereas all landscape configuration metrics showed no significant effects after accounting for land-cover composition. We also detected strong nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous effects: vegetation, water, and albedo interventions generally showed diminishing marginal cooling returns, and the cooling effects of trees, building-height variability, and albedo were strongest in highly built-up or central urban areas. This GRF workflow can support unit-specific and spatially heterogeneous landscape strategies for targeted urban heat mitigation.

title: Space–nature–human associations with land surface temperature across nested planning-spatial units: Evidence from Karst Mountainous Guizhou
abstract: Understanding how urban-spatial, natural, and human-social factors jointly relate to land surface temperature (LST) across nested planning contexts is important for climate-adaptive planning in mountainous cities. Integrated comparisons across planning units that are spatially nested but differ in function, environmental background, and development conditions remain limited. In mountainous karst Guizhou, Southwest China, this study examines the Qianzhong Urban Agglomeration, Guiyang Metropolitan Area, and Gui'an New Area. Hot–cold spot analysis, XGBoost–SHAP, and MGWR are integrated within a space–nature–human (S–N–H) framework to compare LST patterns, model-based variable contributions, nonlinear pairwise interactions, and variable-specific spatial associations under four seasonal–diurnal scenarios. Summer daytime hot spots mainly coincide with built-up areas and development corridors, whereas winter hot spots shift toward western and southern slopes and karst areas; forested mountains and large water bodies remain relatively stable cold spots. Natural-background associations are most prominent in the urban agglomeration, regional gradients coexist with localized built-form and human-activity associations in the metropolitan area, and selected associations become more localized and patchy in the new area, although some remain near-global. S–H, S–N, and N–H interactions vary in direction, magnitude, and response range across planning–spatial and seasonal–diurnal contexts rather than following a uniform cross-level progression. Sensitivity analyses support the principal interpretations across alternative grid resolutions and variable specifications. By linking relative contributions, interaction configurations, and spatial ranges, the framework shifts thermal-environment analysis from isolated factors to context-specific relationships and supports differentiated climate-adaptive planning across nested mountainous planning units.

title: Mapping environmental noise across mainland China using a two-stage stacked ensemble framework
abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified environmental noise in China, yet a national-scale environmental noise exposure map remains absent. This study developed a two-stage stacked ensemble learning framework to map acoustic environments across mainland China and assess socioeconomic disparities in noise exposure. We integrated 554,948 observations from 103,102 environmental noise monitoring stations with multisource geospatial predictors, including transport networks, land use, population density, nighttime lights, GDP, building footprints, points of interest, air pollutants, meteorological variables, elevation, and vegetation. The modelling framework combined Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost as base learners, followed by a LightGBM meta-learner and residual calibration. The final model achieved an R 2 of 0.660, RMSE of 4.720 dB, and MAE of 3.631 dB at the national scale, with performance varying across regions and urbanization strata. The predicted 1 km × 1 km noise maps revealed spatial and temporal gradients, including higher exposure in eastern urban agglomerations and sustained evening-nighttime noise in metropolitan cores. Population-weighted L den declined across GDP per capita quintiles, whereas the proportion of the population exposed to L den >53 dB was highest in the lower-middle group and declined across the higher quintiles. These findings provide macro-scale evidence of environmental noise exposure and inequality in China and support differentiated strategies for sustainable urban noise management.

title: LLM-empowered agents for lifeline network recovery with graph-guided MCP tools
abstract: Post-disaster recovery of lifelines is critical, with numerous studies proposing tools for interdependent lifeline network recovery (LNR). However, existing tools themselves, whether standalone or embedded in systems, lack task-solving capabilities and still depend on human orchestration and execution for handling LNR tasks. Hence, this study proposes a development approach of large language model (LLM)-empowered agents that can intelligently utilize tools to solve LNR tasks. The approach comprises (i) the development of graph-guided LNR tools hosted on model context protocol (MCP) servers, (ii) the construction of LNR agents with the pattern of tool chain generation-tool execution (TCG-TE), and (iii) the evaluation and comparison of agents’ performance. The findings indicate that among the 32 compared agents, 5 out of 8 TCG-TE agents can successfully solve 50 LNR tasks, while none of the 24 traditional agents can solve all tasks. Agents following TCG-TE pattern with graph-guided MCP tools empowered by 8 LLMs solve 13.9% more tasks and reduce 68.2% of unnecessary tool invocations compared to the best-performing agents in traditional patterns. This study contributes by providing a development approach of LNR agents with task-solving capacities. Moreover, the proposed TCG-TE pattern alleviates agents’ difficulty in selecting and orchestrating tools.

title: Quantifying the effects of lift-up building morphology on pedestrian-level wind and comfort in dense urban arrays: A data-driven study
abstract: Pedestrian-level wind (PLW) strongly influences outdoor comfort in high-density cities. Lift-up buildings are widely adopted to enhance near-ground ventilation, yet the nonlinear aerodynamic interactions between their morphology and surrounding urban arrays remain insufficiently quantified. This study develops an integrated framework combining parametric CFD, surrogate modeling, and explainable machine learning to examine how lift-up building morphology influences pedestrian wind environments in dense urban arrays. A dataset of 180 cases was generated for a central lift-up building surrounded by low-rise buildings. The simulations were validated against wind-tunnel measurements, and a Random Forest surrogate model (R² = 0.966) enabled efficient prediction of pedestrian-level wind velocity and pressure-related indicators. Statistical analysis first identifies a morphological control hierarchy in which main-body height shows the strongest association with improved pedestrian-level ventilation, while plan proportions show weaker associations with airflow organization. To further reveal nonlinear relationships, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and one-dimensional accumulated local effects (ALE) were employed. Three key aerodynamic patterns emerge. First, increasing main-body height markedly improves ventilation, but the gains diminish at the upper sampled levels. Second, main-body aspect ratio and plan ratio exhibited non-monotonic responses, with lower unfavorable wind comfort ratios at intermediate values of approximately 1.5–2.0. Third, building height and wind orientation showed a pronounced interaction. Low-rise configurations showed greater contrasts between sampled alignments, whereas taller cases exhibited more favorable and less direction-sensitive pedestrian-level wind conditions. These findings clarify the nonlinear aerodynamic role of lift-up morphology and provide preliminary quantitative guidance for early-stage climate-responsive urban massing design within comparable dense-array settings.

title: Decoding the spatiotemporal cascade effects of compound heat-flood risks in a sinking coastal city: A GCN-LSTM based multi-scenario projection
abstract: Global warming continues to exacerbate compound heat-flood risks in high-density coastal cities yet forecasting their nonlinear spatiotemporal cascade effects under land subsidence regulation remains highly challenging. This study aims to systematically identify the spatiotemporal evolution and underlying driving mechanisms of compound heat-flood risks in Jakarta across various subsidence gradients and future scenarios. We utilized the Hazard-Exposure-Vulnerability framework to quantify historical single and compound risks, specifically the Coupling Coordination Degree (CCD), from 2017 to 2024. Furthermore, a Graph Convolutional Network and Long Short-Term Memory (GCN-LSTM) model, integrated with GeoShapley spatial attribution, was developed to dynamically project risk evolution under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) from the year 2025 to 2050. The results indicate: (1) The compound heat-flood risk exhibits a significant non-linear synergetic pattern, with high-CCD zones remaining primarily concentrated in the northern coastal and central built-up areas, with growing compound risk pressure in the southern HSZ. (2) Impervious surface area acts as the primary anthropogenic driver escalating both hazards, while land subsidence substantially amplifies flood retention and compound stress in the southern region. (3) Multi-scenario projections reveal a structural breakpoint around 2035, after which the risk trajectories under different SSPs diverge more clearly. (4) Differentiated spatial interventions balance local geological constraints, enabling the highly vulnerable high subsidence zones (HSZ) to achieve the most significant risk mitigation. Ultimately, prioritizing localized groundwater control and spatial ecological renewal is absolutely crucial for cutting the destructive cascade transmission and achieving resilient urban development.

title: Environmental justice and urban heat thresholds in Istanbul: An explainable machine learning approach with spatial residual diagnostics
abstract: Rapid urbanization intensifies the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, yet neighborhood-level surface thermal exposure remains unevenly distributed across urban populations. While the environmental justice dimensions of UHI have received attention in Global North contexts, empirical evidence from rapidly developing megacities remains limited, and conventional machine learning applications in urban climatology frequently overlook spatial autocorrelation, risking biased inference. To address these gaps, this study develops a hybrid spatial machine learning framework to examine the drivers of mean summer Land Surface Temperature (LST)—a radiometric surface temperature proxy, not a direct measure of thermal comfort—across 750 neighborhoods in Istanbul. An XGBoost regressor was integrated with a post-hoc Spatial Error Model (SEM) diagnostic filter, reducing residual Moran's I from 0.449 (p = 0.001) to −0.011 (p = 0.321) under a district-grouped spatial cross-validation design (Test R² = 0.937; CV R² = 0.870 ± 0.070). SHAP analysis was applied to a 25-variable dataset fusing Landsat 8/9 remote sensing imagery, NASA SRTM topographic data, and neighborhood-level socioeconomic records to quantify non-linear feature contributions to LST. NDBI and NDVI emerged as the primary morphological determinants, followed by distance to coastline and population density. A density-dependent vegetation efficacy transition band was estimated at approximately 27,000–34,000 persons/km² (primary breakpoint estimate: 28,070; bootstrap 95% CI: 27,176–30,744; district-grouped spatial sensitivity range: 26,914–34,312 persons/km²), above which NDVI cooling contributions diminish substantially regardless of greenness level. A systematic thermal disparity was identified across socioeconomic groups: A+ (elite) neighborhoods exhibited a mean summer LST of 39.4 °C, compared with 42.8 °C in D (low SES) neighborhoods (Δ = 3.4 °C), indicating an associational thermal gradient along socioeconomic lines. These findings suggest that urban greening strategies should be calibrated to local population-density transition bands, and that surface heat mitigation planning should explicitly account for the unequal spatial distribution of surface thermal exposure across socioeconomic groups.

title: Fine-scale urban heat mapping by machine learning downscaling of MODIS land surface temperature in a hyper-arid megacity
abstract: Fine-scale land surface temperature (LST) underpins assessment of the surface urban heat island and heat exposure in cities, yet thermal sensors trade spatial detail against temporal frequency. Evaluate a reproducible machine learning framework that downscales seasonal-median MODIS daytime LST from 1 km to 100 m over the hyper-arid megacity of Greater Cairo, Egypt, for summer 2025. A scale-consistent regression of coarse LST on fine predictors—Sentinel-2 indices, terrain derivatives, and sub-pixel ESA WorldCover fractions—is combined with an additive residual correction; seven algorithms are compared. Products are assessed by cross-validation, scale-consistency on re-aggregation, and comparison with Landsat-8/9. At the coarse scale the predictor–LST relationship is strong (histogram gradient boosting: R² = 0.94, RMSE = 0.77 °C; 0.93–0.92 under 3–8 km blocking); re-aggregation shows approximate MODIS consistency (R² = 0.83–0.99, model-dependent; small bias for signal-consistent models); and the 100 m fields recover the intra-urban thermal pattern. Against Landsat, however, every product consistent with the coarse signal shows a large systematic cold bias (−5.5 to −6.1 °C) and a negative R², while retaining moderate spatial correlation (r up to 0.84); the bias is minimal over water and largest over built-up and bare surfaces. The un-downscaled MODIS field carries the same offset (−5.93 °C), as do twelve same-day pairs (−6.3 ± 2.0 °C), so it is inherited from the MODIS–Landsat product pair to within the empirically measured scale-consistency error, rather than being created by sharpening. Statistical sharpening faithfully redistributes the parent sensor’s information but cannot reconcile inter-sensor differences; a non-coincident finer image is not a valid absolute reference for downscaled urban LST.

title: Towards an urban digital twin: An XAI-integrated prototype framework for sustainable mobility modelling in Algiers, Algeria
abstract: Rapid urbanisation across North African metropolises—Algiers in particular—places transport systems under mounting stress: congestion erodes economic productivity, vehicle emissions degrade public health, and energy-intensive mobility patterns accelerate carbon expenditure. These pressures are compounded by the absence of interpretable tools capable of jointly quantifying congestion, energy demand, and air quality in forms actionable for governance. This underscores the need for integrated spatiotemporal modeling of traffic congestion, energy demand, and air quality for sustainable urban mobility planning. This study constructs, validates, and applies a prototype framework towards an Urban Digital Twin for Algiers, integrating eight heterogeneous urban data streams within a unified geospatial environment to jointly model traffic congestion, energy demand, and air quality. A comprehensive hybrid dataset, comprising directly observed and statistically augmented records for model robustness, encompasses 500,000 spatiotemporal records across 5,000 road segments and 57 communes. Random Forest and XGBoost models were benchmarked with SHAP attribution and scenario simulation. The proposed framework provides an exploratory, scenario-based decision-support tool directly applicable to the ongoing revision in Algiers. The Compact Mixed-Use and TOD scenarios demonstrate substantial energy and environmental gains—energy reduction and NO2 improvement—establishing a scenario-based, quantitative evidence base for transit-integrated land use revisions to Algiers' master planning frameworks, utilizing a hybrid dataset comprising both directly observed and statistically augmented records to directly inform temporally targeted demand management policy for North African cities.

title: A continental-scale XGBoost framework for multi-hazard susceptibility and socioeconomic exposure in South America
abstract: Floods, droughts, and wildfires affect many South American cities, but continent-scale assessments rarely connect hazard susceptibility with urban exposure. We present a continental-scale (∼1 km) framework that compares a simple weighted benchmark with hazard-specific Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models built from 27 Earth observation and socioeconomic datasets. On identical held-out test pixels, XGBoost increased ROC-AUC from 0.65 to 0.93 for flood, from 0.59 to 0.89 for drought, and from 0.74 to 0.92 for wildfire, with similar gains in PR-AUC, F1 score, and balanced accuracy. We therefore used XGBoost to generate the final susceptibility maps. The mapped classes are relative continental quantile classes, not absolute event probability thresholds. The mapped patterns place higher flood likelihood in humid lowlands and river corridors, higher drought likelihood in water-limited hot regions, and higher wildfire likelihood in hot, dry frontier regions. A city-scale synthesis for 758 South American cities places the strongest combinations of high composite hazard and lower adaptive capacity in northeastern Brazil, Caribbean-facing Colombia and Venezuela, and lowland Bolivia, while lower-hazard and stronger-capacity settings are more common in parts of the Southern Cone and Andean corridors. The maps, input layers, municipal classes, and city-level summaries can be explored in MIRA, the Multi-hazard Index for Risk Assessment, at https://riskframeworksa.github.io/data_viewer/.

title: Urban wind field reconstruction for low-altitude flight: A comparison of Gappy POD and deep autoencoder strategies using CFD and sparse sensing
abstract: Urban wind field reconstruction from sparse observations is important for real-time monitoring, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) flight safety, and smart city applications. However, accurately recovering complex wind fields in dense urban areas remains challenging because building-induced flow distortion creates strong spatial heterogeneity. In this study, four reconstruction frameworks, namely Gappy Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), Gappy POD combined with fully-connected Neural Networks (POD+NN), Autoencoder (AE), and AE combined with NN (AE+NN), are developed and evaluated for sparse sensor urban wind field reconstruction using a high-resolution CFD database for a central district in Shenzhen. The results show that deep learning-based methods outperform the traditional linear Gappy POD approach, with AE+NN achieving the best overall accuracy and robustness. At 120 m height, which is highly relevant to low-altitude UAV applications, AE+NN reduces wind speed reconstruction errors by about 20–30% compared with Gappy POD. AE+NN also remains stable under sparse sensor configurations, whereas Gappy POD requires substantially more sensors to avoid large errors. Reconstruction accuracy is strongly influenced by height and wind direction, while the effect of sensor layout (randomly or uniformly distributed) is comparatively small. AE-based methods show stronger generalization across wind directions and better reproduce local wind variations and wake-affected regions along representative UAV trajectories. In addition, introducing a physics-based regularization term improves the spatial consistency of AE reconstruction by reducing physically inconsistent solutions and narrowing the full-field error distribution. This study demonstrates that combining nonlinear manifold learning with latent-variable prediction provides an efficient and accurate framework for sparse sensor urban wind reconstruction. The proposed AE+NN approach shows strong potential for practical applications such as UAV route planning, urban wind hazard assessment, and smart-city wind monitoring.

title: MTML-EV: Multi-target meta-learning for cross-zone urban electric vehicle charging infrastructure management
abstract: Rapid electric vehicle (EV) adoption is reshaping urban mobility and energy systems, intensifying challenges for charging infrastructure management, including congestion, uneven spatial demand, and grid stress. Addressing these challenges requires reliable forecasting of multiple charging-system states across both near-real-time operation and short-term planning horizons, particularly for newly deployed or evolving zones with limited historical data. Existing urban EV charging forecasting approaches often focus on individual charging-system variables and exhibit limited adaptability to previously unseen zones. To address this limitation, this paper presents MTML-EV, a multi-target meta-learning framework that jointly predicts charging occupancy, energy demand, and electricity price across 1-, 6-, and 12-hour forecasting horizons. MTML-EV formulates each traffic zone as a learning task and leverages a BiGRU-based temporal encoder optimized with first-order model-agnostic meta-learning (FOMAML) to learn transferable temporal representations that enable rapid adaptation to previously unseen zones. Extensive experiments on the UrbanEV benchmark evaluate MTML-EV across multiple forecasting horizons and unseen-zone adaptation scenarios against deep learning, hybrid, and Transformer-based baselines. For 1-hour ahead prediction on unseen zones, MTML-EV reduces RMSE by 7.5% for energy demand and 59% for electricity price compared with the strongest Transformer baseline while maintaining high occupancy forecasting accuracy. Additional robustness analyses across multiple unseen-zone partitions demonstrate that these performance gains remain stable under varying zone configurations, while interpretability analysis confirms that the model relies on meaningful temporal, charging-related, and contextual factors. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of MTML-EV for multi-target cross-zone forecasting under heterogeneous urban conditions, highlighting the value of transferable temporal representations for adaptive EV charging infrastructure management.

title: Optimizing urban green space spatial pattern to reduce land surface temperature: A greedy-based adaptive strategy
abstract: Urban green space (UGS) planning often draws on average relationships between spatial configuration and land surface temperature (LST), whereas phased interventions require choices for specific locations and landscape states. This study compares three predefined greening rules with a greedy-based adaptive strategy (AS) in Philadelphia. A CNN-XGBoost model provides a common scenario-evaluation engine; the adaptive decision procedure selects among centralized, irregular, and decentralized rules for each planning unit and round. The original 420 m group-based split yielded a test R² of 0.909. An additional validation excluding overlapping predictor windows yielded a mean R² of 0.886, providing a more conservative assessment of within-city prediction. Under the stated scenario assumptions, AS achieved the greatest cumulative predicted cooling and the highest average cooling efficiency, 0.159°C per percentage-point increase in UGS cover. This efficiency exceeded those of the irregular, decentralized, random-switching, and centralized strategies by 12.0%, 14.4%, 25.2%, and 57.4%, respectively. In the reference allocation, 72% of planning units changed their selected rule at least once over four rounds. Repetition and sensitivity analyses supported the comparative advantage of AS across the tested settings. The findings support reassessing a defined set of greening alternatives as local conditions and implementation stages change, providing a practical framework for adaptive scenario comparison during phased urban greening.

title: Research on spatial heterogeneity of urban flood susceptibility and model attribution in Beijing: An XGBoost-SHAP analysis based on spatial cross-validation
abstract: Urban waterlogging exhibits significant spatial autocorrelation and extreme class imbalance, which may lead to overestimation of model generalization performance when random data splits are used. Taking 68,104 500 m grid cells in Beijing as evaluation units, this study constructs an urban waterlogging susceptibility model based on 405 historically waterlogged positive samples and 16 static geo-socioeconomic indicators covering hazard, exposure, and vulnerability. Fivefold spatial block cross-validation at 0.1° resolution is employed to compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Linear SVM, LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost, together with class-imbalance handling techniques including class weighting, SMOTE, Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, Balanced Random Forest, and EasyEnsemble. Results show that XGBoost achieves a spatial cross-validation ROC-AUC of 0.888±0.020 and a PR-AUC of 0.052±0.011, with a recall of 0.796±0.067 for the waterlogging class. Although it attains the highest PR-AUC among all models, its precision is only 0.024, indicating that the model is better suited as a high-recall screening tool than as a deterministic forecasting system. ROC-AUC values across the three pseudo-negative sampling strategies range from 0.882 to 0.887, and the SHAP rankings of slope, population density, and vegetation coverage remain generally stable. Full-sample SHAP attribution identifies slope, vegetation coverage, total population, and elevation as the most influential variables. Breakpoints derived from piecewise regression are interpreted as internal statistical associations within the model rather than as hydrological or planning thresholds. . Street typology based on 19 aggregated indicators retained eight principal components explaining 92.3% of variance. Although K=2 achieved the highest silhouette coefficient (0.375), the K=5 solution was retained for governance-oriented classification because its seed stability was high (mean ARI = 0.991) and its 80% subsample stability remained acceptable (ARI = 0.891 ± 0.090). Its silhouette coefficient was 0.221, so it is not presented as the unique statistical optimum. This study repositions the model from "risk prediction" to "static susceptibility identification," while explicitly acknowledging limitations arising from unobserved factors such as drainage network capacity, pumping station performance, event rainfall characteristics, and monitoring biases.

title: Dual friction mapping of urban pedestrian spaces: Integrating street-view visual analytics and Geographically Neural Network Weighted Regression in Izmir, Türkiye
