abstract: Pedestrian comfort is undermined both by physical obstructions that compress usable sidewalk space and by thermal stress in hot weather. Yet physical and thermal friction are usually measured separately, leaving planners without a fine-grained basis for deciding where obstacle removal, sidewalk widening, or shade and cooling interventions are actually needed. This study introduces the Pedestrian Friction Index (PFI), combining a Physical Comfort Score (visual obstruction from street-view imagery, including effective clear walking width) and a Thermal Friction Score (land surface temperature, albedo, greenery, and sky openness) in equal measure, applied across 5663 street-view points in Izmir, Türkiye. Street-view images were segmented for physical indicators, while satellite imagery supplied thermal and terrain metrics. We modelled PFI using Geographically Neural Network Weighted Regression (GNNWR), allowing spatial non-stationarity across the city, and benchmarked it against four spatial regression models. GNNWR achieved an out-of-sample R2 of 0.407 under repeated hex-blocked cross-validation. Local coefficients indicated that clear walking width and tree canopy height consistently reduced friction, whereas morphological density, street canyon ratio, ground coverage, and park distance increased it in specific spatial contexts. A bivariate vulnerability atlas identified locations where high physical and thermal friction coincide, guiding sidewalk widening, obstacle removal, tree planting, and heat mitigation in Mediterranean cities. The findings support a planning transition from generic walkability rankings to diagnosis-specific pedestrian infrastructure policy.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution and spatially heterogeneous drivers of urban flood risk: A K-means optimized XGBoost model
abstract: With the intensification of climate change and rapid urbanization, urban flooding events have become increasingly frequent, posing serious threats to urban safety and sustainable development. However, existing studies often regard cities as homogeneous spaces, which limits the understanding of spatially heterogeneous flood drivers. Taking the Ningbo urban area as the study area, historical urban flood points from 2010 to 2024 collected from social media and government websites were analyzed using kernel density estimation and standard deviational ellipse analysis to reveal spatiotemporal evolution patterns. Based on flood records and multisource influencing factors, a K-means optimized XGBoost (KXGBoost) model was developed, combined with SHAP and Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) analyses to interpret the contributions and nonlinear response patterns of key factors across different zones. The results show that high and very high risk areas were mainly distributed in the central urban area, and the spatial pattern of urban flooding evolved from a highly concentrated monocentric pattern toward a more dispersed and polycentric pattern. The KXGBoost model considering spatial heterogeneity improved the AUC from 0.84 to 0.89 compared with the baseline XGBoost model. The highly urbanized Zone 1 was mainly influenced by Drainage, Road and NDVI, whereas Zone 3 showed higher contributions from NDVI, Road and MBH. PDP results further revealed nonlinear relationships of drainage density and vegetation coverage with flood risk, and these response patterns varied under different road and building conditions. These findings provide scientific support for differentiated urban flood management strategies and enhance urban resilience under climate change.

title: From optimization to generation: A machine learning and morphology-constrained GAN framework for improving energy and thermal performance in residential clusters
abstract: Urban morphology substantially affects energy and thermal performance in residential clusters. However, existing studies have mainly focused on performance prediction or parametric optimization, with limited attention to translating optimized parameters into spatial layout solutions. This study proposes an optimization-generation framework that combines machine learning and a morphology-constrained generative adversarial network (MCGAN) for residential clusters. Using 5466 samples from five representative climate zones in China, four performance indicators were computed: energy use intensity (EUI), solar energy generation intensity (SEGI), net energy use intensity (NEUI), and outdoor thermal comfort autonomy (OTCA). Machine learning-based surrogate models and SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) analysis were used to predict performance and identify dominant morphological drivers. The best-performing surrogate model was integrated with the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) and MCGAN to generate residential layouts from optimized morphological parameters. The results indicate that energy-related indicators are mainly influenced by the perimeter-to-area ratio and facade-to-roof area ratio, whereas outdoor thermal comfort is primarily governed by the sky view factor and buildings enclosure ratio. XGBoost and LightGBM achieved the highest predictive accuracy, with R² values exceeding 0.89 across all indicators. A residential cluster in Wuhan was used to validate the proposed framework, where 1211 candidate layouts were generated and 161 Pareto-optimal solutions were identified through the optimization-to-generation process. Equal-weight TOPSIS evaluation of the re-simulation results indicated that the optimized schemes achieved better overall performance than the original design. The proposed framework provides interpretable decision support for early-stage residential cluster planning and design.

title: Investigating the Nonlinear and Spatially Heterogeneous Impacts of Urban Form on Land Surface Temperature Using Geographic Explainable Artificial Intelligence
abstract:
ABSTRACT
Previous studies have extensively examined urban form–land surface temperature (LST) relationships. However, nonlinear responses, spatiotemporal heterogeneity, and local predictive contributions have not been adequately examined within a unified framework. This study examines these relationships in Sana’a City, Yemen, using multi-temporal Landsat data from 2005, 2015, and 2025 within a geographically and temporally weighted random forest–GeoShapley (GTWRF–GeoShapley) framework. The analysis distinguishes local linear sensitivity, unsigned local random-forest importance, and signed predictive attribution. Results indicate that elevated LST has progressively expanded from the urban core into developing peripheral zones, with the area exceeding 25°C increasing from 22% to 47%. Spatially, regions of grid cells dominated by built-environment indicators increased from 28% to 50%, while the proportion dominated by vegetation-related indicators declined from 72% to 50%. Positive contributions associated with the Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI) and built-up density (BUD) became increasingly spatially contiguous across central built-up areas; the mean absolute GeoShapley contribution of NDBI increased from 0.52 to 0.60°C, while BUD remained stable at approximately 0.50°C. Urban compactness exhibited a localized core–periphery pattern, with the largest proportional increase in mean absolute contribution (+25.0%). Conversely, cooling contributions associated with vegetation fraction became increasingly fragmented and were largely confined to less urbanized peripheral areas. Furthermore, BUD exhibited a nonlinear warming response, with its positive contribution increasing from +1.2 to +1.6°C beyond an empirical transition near 30% BUD. These findings provide geographically explicit insights for managing urban growth. Strategies aimed at preventing fragmented built-up expansion from reducing connected green spaces and generating localized thermal hotspots could help curb fragmented urban expansion at city fringes, ultimately supporting sustainable morphological transitions for rapidly growing cities.
keywords: Geographically and temporally weighted random forest

title: Air-quality-sensitive urban design on NO2 Mitigation in the high-rise high-density City of London: A machine-learning land-use regression analysis
abstract: Elevated nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) remains a persistent urban air-quality and public-health concern. In the UK, despite progressive emissions-control policies, exceedances have historically occurred in central London. This study quantifies neighbourhood-scale NO₂ variability in the high-rise, high-density City of London and evaluates how air-quality-sensitive urban design, alongside traffic measures, influences concentrations in a morphology-constrained street network. We developed machine-learning land-use regression (LUR) models to predict NO₂ distribution: the Random Forest (RF) model performed best (adjusted R² = 0.88; RMSE = 7.6 μg m⁻³; MAE = 6.25 μg m⁻³). The RF-LUR model was then applied to assess air-quality-sensitive urban design scenarios. Increased built fraction associated with population growth was associated with widespread NO₂ increases (up to 5.5 µg m⁻³), consistent with reduced dispersion in dense street-canyons. A 50% reduction in heavy-vehicle activity was associated with corridor-focused NO₂ decreases of 1–6 µg m⁻³. Introducing additional high-rise buildings increased height variability and was associated with NO₂ reductions up to ∼7 µg m⁻³ in the eastern cluster. Targeted tree-canopy expansion was associated with hotspot reductions of up to ∼4 µg m⁻³ but produced small local increases in some areas. The combined intervention package was associated with the largest overall improvement, with NO 2 reductions up to ∼7 µg m⁻³. The results show that integrating urban morphology within machine-learning LUR models can provide a practical, fine-scale evidence base for spatial targeting and comparative appraisal of NO₂ mitigation options in high-density urban districts.

title: Deep reinforcement learning-based UAV navigation in 3D urban boundary layers
abstract: Low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) navigation in urban environments is challenged by complex building geometry and unsteady wind disturbances, including wakes, recirculation, and vertical motions within the urban boundary layer (UBL). To improve autonomous navigation under partial observation and unsteady wind disturbances, this study proposes a Latent actor and Random Network Distillation (RND) augmented Soft actor critic method (LARA-SAC). A high-fidelity three-dimensional (3D) unsteady urban wind field generated by large-eddy simulation (LES) is incorporated into the navigation environment, enabling the agent to learn continuous control policies under explicit building constraints and wind forcing. LARA-SAC integrates historical observation memory, latent trajectory exploration, and state action novelty estimation within the SAC framework. A history queue and a Gated Transformer eXtra Large (GTrXL) encoder extract recent wind disturbances, target direction changes, and obstacle approach trends, while latent exploration improves directional consistency and RND enhances early value learning through novelty feedback. Compared with recent benchmark methods, LARA-SAC shows more stable learning behavior, stronger task completion ability, and lower collision risk. The learned policy adapts both horizontal motion and flight altitude according to the target position, building layout, and local wind variations, rather than following fixed routes. Additional energy and generalization tests further indicate that LARA-SAC maintains safe and continuous navigation in larger urban wind fields, demonstrating good stability, safety, and adaptability in complex 3D urban environments.

title: Explainable AI for targeted green infrastructure allocation: A predictive framework for urban heat island mitigation
abstract: Semi-arid cities, where vegetation is scarce and thermal vulnerability is increasing, are particularly exposed to urban heat island (UHI) effects. This study develops an explainable machine-learning framework for prioritising urban greening in a semi-arid city, applied to Shiraz, Iran. The target is the local surface thermal anomaly, derived from Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 surface temperature over the summers of 2013 to 2022 at 90 m support, predicted from 72 vegetation, built-up, land-cover, population, proximity, topographic, spectral and building-height predictors that exclude absolute surface temperature. Under random ten-fold resampling (map completion within the sampled city) gradient boosting reaches R² = 0.879; under buffered spatial block cross-validation (transfer to unseen parts of the city) it reaches a fold-mean R² of 0.648 (RMSE 1.76°C), and five tree-ensemble implementations agree within 0.01. SHAP attribution identifies the bare-land fraction and population density as the leading predictors and the anthropogenic, proximity and landscape-configuration predictors as the leading family. Hotspot detection recovers 42.5 % of the hottest decile of cells at equal treated area, a 5.6-fold improvement over random siting, and conformal prediction intervals cover 0.874 of held-out cells at a nominal 0.90. Five greening allocation strategies are compared at equal treated area; under the predictor-update rule tested, an area-of-applicability test places 15 to 98 % of treated cells outside the domain of the fitted model, so no cooling magnitude is reported. The framework gives a transparent basis for targeting green infrastructure in semi-arid cities and identifies when data-driven cooling estimates should not be used.

title: Satellite-derived LST can overstate vegetation cooling benefits: Evidence from surface and air temperature analyses in Sydney
abstract: Urban vegetation cooling is often assessed using satellite-derived land surface temperature (LST) and individual vegetation indicators. However, it remains unclear whether relationships between different vegetation indicators and LST are reflected in near-surface air temperature (Ta), and how they vary across seasons, between day and night, and along the coastal–inland gradient. Using an integrated 2019–2025 framework for Sydney, this study combines LST, dense Ta observations, vegetation indicators, urban morphology, and coastal proximity. Statistical and machine-learning analyses quantify bivariate and multivariate relationships and rank predictor contributions. We find from the multivariate analysis that the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), a greenness proxy, is strongly associated with lower daytime LST, leading to a −1.92°C reduction in summer and −1.78°C in spring per 0.1-unit increase. In contrast, NDVI is related to lower Ta only during summer daytime, with a smaller impact (−0.18°C per 0.1-unit increase), indicating that NDVI–LST patterns are weakly reflected in Ta. For air temperature, Leaf Area Index (LAI) anomaly is the leading summer vegetation predictor, leading to a −0.68°C reduction during daytime and −0.46°C at night per 0.1-unit increase, although LAI–temperature relationships reverse in winter. Summer feature importance reinforces this contrast, with NDVI ranking highest for LST and LAI anomaly ranking highest for Ta. Overall, LST-based vegetation–temperature relationships can overstate Ta responses with variation across vegetation indicators and along the coastal-inland gradient. Heat-adaptation planning should distinguish surface-temperature responses from Ta responses and combine greenness with canopy-structure metrics.

title: Monitoring and forecasting of urban air pollution and exceedance events: implications for environmental risk assessment and early warning communication using machine learning in sustainable cities
abstract: Short-term pollution episodes are often hidden by annual-average reporting, and machine-learning forecasts are rarely benchmarked against persistence or evaluated at the 24-h/8-h periods defining regulatory exceedance. This study analyses 15,502 hourly observations (Nov. 2024-Aug. 2026) of PM 2.5 , PM 10 , NO 2 , NO, NO x , O 3 and SO 2 at an urban background station in Iasi, Romania. Random Forest and XGBoost were trained at three horizons (1, 6, 24 h) via season-balanced walk-forward validation, and separately to forecast next-day (D+1) regulatory indicators. PM 2.5 , PM 10 and NO 2 complied with current EU limits (2008/50/EC) in 2025 but exceeded WHO 2021 guidelines 1.5-2.9x and already exceed 2030 EU limits (Directive 2024/2881). At 1 h, persistence matched or exceeded both models for every pollutant (O 3 R² = 0.87 vs. 0.81 for XGBoost), relative skill versus persistence became positive for most pollutants at 6 h, but remained horizon and pollutant-dependent thereafter. Direct D+1 forecasts achieved modest skill (R² = -0.27 to 0.22), with persistence matching or exceeding XGBoost for four of five indicators, SO2 excepted. Event-based validation showed usable detection for PM2.5 and NO2 (POD 0.67-0.85 and 0.75-0.87 respectively) but XGBoost detected none of 39 ozone exceedances at the WHO threshold, versus 64% for persistence. These results show machine-learning value is horizon and pollutant-dependent, not automatic: persistence remains highly competitive, and for ozone superior. The contribution is methodological: season-balanced validation, horizon/averaging-period reconciliation, and event-based validation against naive baselines.

title: Forecasting Urban Heat Island hotspots using spatially aware machine learning: Explainable multi-model prediction with spatial validation and uncertainty analysis
abstract: Urban Heat Island (UHI) hotspot forecasting is essential for proactive climate-resilient urban planning, yet existing machine learning approaches often overlook spatial dependence, temporal dynamics, and prediction uncertainty. This study proposes a spatio-temporal GeoAI framework for forecasting future UHI hotspot distributions in Gautam Buddha Nagar (Noida–Greater Noida), India, using multi-temporal Landsat observations from 2018, 2020, 2023, and 2025. Five environmental variables, namely the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), Land Surface Temperature (LST), and UHI intensity, were derived using Google Earth Engine(GEE). To characterize the spatial structure of urban thermal patterns, the framework integrates Global Moran’s I, Getis–Ord Gi*, and Ripley’s L-function, providing complementary assessments of spatial autocorrelation, hotspot localization, and multi-scale clustering. Spatial-lag and temporal-change (Δ) features were further engineered to explicitly capture neighbourhood interactions and temporal evolution. Five forecasting models representing feature-based (Random Forest and XGBoost) and sequence-based (LSTM, Transformer, and SSM-Mamba) learning paradigms were evaluated using ten independent random seeds. Performance was assessed using Accuracy, Macro-F1, Cohen’s κ, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). XGBoost achieved the best overall performance, attaining an Accuracy of 98.9%, Macro-F1 of 0.924, Cohen’s κof 0.881, and MCC of 0.883. Ablation experiments showed that focal loss improved the sequence models; spatial-lag features were retained to represent neighbourhood conditions. SHAP analysis identified built-up intensity, vegetation, neighbourhood interactions, and temporal-change variables as the main associations used by the models of hotspot evolution. Agreement between SHAP explanations and Getis–Ord Gi∗ maps was moderate. A multi-model consensus layer, checked on labelled 2025 cells, was applied to a 2027 projection. No ground truth exists for 2027, so that map is an unvalidated scenario. The framework is an interpretable, spatially checked forecasting audit for this district.

title: Nonlinear and heterogeneous effects of 2D/3D factors on global urban heat island using explainable spatial machine learning
abstract: Although global research communities widely acknowledge the significant challenges posed by the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, existing studies seldom simultaneously investigate the nonlinear and spatially non-stationary effects of 2D/3D factors on Surface UHI Intensity (SUHII) at the global scale. This study employed an explainable spatial machine learning framework that integrates Geographically Weighted Random Forests (GW-RF) and Shapley values to explore the complex effects of 2D/3D factors on SUHII across 2488 cities worldwide. Results reveal that mean SUHII varied significantly across continents, ranging from 1.201 °C in Africa to 2.121 °C in North America. Among 2D factors, rural vegetation ratio and urban impervious surface fraction are the most important drivers of SUHII, whereas among 3D factors, rural elevation and urban building height variability are the most important. Nonlinear analysis indicates that the percentage of urban building footprint has a positive effect on SUHII when it exceeds 16%, whereas building height variability exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship, with positive effects mainly between 3 and 10 m. Spatially non-stationary analysis indicated that urban impervious surface fraction has a greater influence in Eastern North America, Eastern Asia, and Central South America, whereas rural vegetation ratio exerts a stronger influence in European and Asian cities. Furthermore, urban irregularity has a strong effect in megacities, and the percentage of building footprint is influential in inland cities. These insights support the design of targeted, localized measures to counteract UHI.

title: A comparative machine learning assessment for urban flood susceptibility modeling and future flood susceptibility projections in Dhaka Metropolitan Area (DMA), Bangladesh
abstract: Rapid urbanization and changing rainfall patterns are exacerbating flood-related issues in growing megacities. This study assessed flood susceptibility considering 17 Sentinel-1 flood events, 1451 modeling samples, and 13 conditioning factors to compare three standard ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM) with spatial cross-validation. Model interpretation was informed by SHAP and accumulated local effects. Scenario-based projections through 2060 under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 were supported by four climate models from CMIP6 and CA-Markov land-cover simulations. In the reported classifier comparison, LightGBM achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.969 and an F1-score of 0.861, with a mean spatial cross-validation ROC-AUC of 0.954. The primary predictive factors were elevation, rainfall, and nearness to rivers. In the baseline scenario, 35.01% of Dhaka was highly and very highly susceptible. Projected built-up coverage increased from 63% in 2040 to 76.1% in 2060. In 2051-2060, high and very high susceptibility shares were reported as 38.82% under SSP2-4.5 and 45.01% under SSP5-8.5, with persistent concentrations in the eastern and southeastern parts of Dhaka. Long-term interpretation is limited by uncertainties in land-cover hindcasting, climate projections, and unrepresented drainage operations. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrated geospatial modeling to identify flood susceptibility hotspots and support climate-resilient urban planning through flood-sensitive zoning, wetland conservation, and targeted drainage improvements.

title: Temporal non-stationarity limits urban heat model transferability: Evidence from interpretable spatial machine learning across ten highly urbanized bay areas (1990–2022)
abstract: Urban heat assessments inform long-term land-use and adaptation decisions, yet the relationships on which they rely may change as cities evolve. We examined the temporal stability of land surface temperature (LST) relationships across ten highly urbanized bay areas during 1990–2022, using seven historical stages, 70 spatially validated XGBoost–SHAP models and 210 forward-transfer tests. Results show that: (1) Mean hot-season LST increased in nine bay areas, with endpoint changes ranging from −0.5 to +5.4 °C. (2) Five bay areas experienced changes in their dominant predictors. Natural-surface importance was higher on average in Global North cases (p = 0.063), whereas topographic importance was higher in Global South cases (p = 0.032). (3) Nonlinear SHAP contribution positions varied across historical stages, while clustering identified two broad long-term predictor pathways. (4) Of the 210 forward transfers, 208 underperformed their paired target-stage models. Mean R² was 0.434 versus 0.876, a difference of −0.442 (95% bay-bootstrap confidence interval −0.643 to −0.279). Intercept recalibration increased mean R² to 0.788, although 207 transfers still underperformed, with a residual difference of −0.088 (−0.122 to −0.059). Explanatory structures showed partial persistence, with mean Top-3 overlap of 0.706 and rank correlation of 0.748. Overall, these findings reveal that historical LST models can retain recognizable explanatory structures while experiencing substantial losses in predictive accuracy. Regular evaluation of historical models against updated thermal observations can inform model recalibration and support more responsive urban heat adaptation planning.

title: HeatVision: Estimating human-centric radiative flux using physics-informed computer vision
abstract: Physics-based models to simulate radiative flux in an urban environment, a key driver of human body energy balances and heat stress, are limited by computational load and data availability, while purely “data-driven” AI approaches lack interpretability and robustness. To address this gap, we introduce HeatVision, a physics-informed computer vision framework that leverages widely available street-view imagery and meteorological data to estimate complex radiative fluxes. It employs computer vision algorithms trained on infrared thermography to transform optical images into synthetic infrared imagery, enabling pixel-wise integration of heat losses/gains across a 360°spherical projection. We validated the approach using 790 paired infrared-optical imagery taken in Hong Kong. HeatVision’s estimates of the mean radiant temperature (MRT) agreed reasonably well with measured data from a globe thermometer (with a MAE of 2.31 °C and an RMSE of 3.48 °C), outperforming a physics-based simulation tool (CityComfort+) in both robustness and computational efficiency. By combining physical principles with computer vision, HeatVision demonstrates that the longwave radiation component of urban radiative flux can be estimated from street-view imagery without 3D urban models. However, extending the vision-based approach to shortwave radiation, and validating across more cities and seasons still remains the primary directions for future work.

title: SHAP-informed and uncertainty-aware urban flood susceptibility mapping for planning support: a CatBoost framework
abstract: Urban flooding is a major hazard in Iranian cities, and Shiraz is repeatedly affected due to its topography, rapid urban expansion, and drainage limitations. We produced a 10 × 10 m urban flood-susceptibility map for Shiraz and interpreted key controls using machine learning and SHAP. A 2000–2020 inventory included 220 flooded and 220 non-flooded locations. Sixteen predictors were derived from multi-source layers and grouped into climatic, geographic, urban-development, and infrastructure factors (e.g., rainfall, elevation, slope, TWI, drainage density, distance to rivers, land use, and soil texture). Multicollinearity was checked using VIF, tolerance, and Pearson correlation. Six classifiers RF, KNN, GBM, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost were evaluated using complementary holdout and geographically grouped spatial-validation protocols. CatBoost achieved a holdout AUC of 0.9089 and an F1-score of 0.8593, while repeated 5-km spatial cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.8588. The final CatBoost map classified 43.60% of the study area as having high or very high flood susceptibility. SHAP analysis identified rainfall, distance to rivers, TWI, and slope as influential predictors. The susceptibility surface achieved a success-rate AUC of 0.874, and full high-susceptibility agreement among all six models covered 32.39% of the study area. The resulting uncertainty-aware planning-priority map provides spatial screening information for field verification, river-corridor assessment, and drainage evaluation, subject to site-specific engineering validation.

title: Uncertainty-aware graph neural reconstruction of urban temperature fields from sparse sensors under deployment constraints
abstract: Reconstructing spatially continuous daily temperature fields from sparse observations is important for environmental monitoring and heat-risk analysis, yet practical deployments are limited by sensor availability and spacing constraints. This study presents an uncertainty-aware graph neural network framework that combines mean-residual graph-attention reconstruction, deployment-constrained sensor placement, and probabilistic temperature-threshold mapping. The gridded reference field is first evaluated against independent in situ observations to establish its suitability and scale of interpretation. Reconstruction performance is then assessed using separated training, validation, and held-out test periods, supplemented by leave-one-year-out evaluation across alternative sensor budgets and placement strategies. Comparisons include inverse-distance weighting, validation-tuned kriging, a Matérn Gaussian process, residual Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, and a sensor-mean baseline. The proposed model generally achieves the lowest missing-node reconstruction errors at moderate and larger sensor budgets, whereas residual POD remains competitive under the most restrictive sensing configuration. The benefits of additional sensors diminish as the network becomes denser, and the relative performance of placement strategies depends on both the sensor budget and reconstruction method. The ensemble formulation provides spatially varying predictive uncertainty, separates within-member and between-member contributions, and supports calibrated prediction intervals and spatial exceedance-probability mapping. Overall, the framework provides a basis for resource-aware reconstruction of daily grid-scale temperature fields and for evaluating environmental sensor-network designs under practical deployment constraints.

title: Optimization-guided residual reinforcement learning for real-time low-carbon dispatch of user-side battery–ice hybrid energy storage systems
abstract: High renewable energy penetration increases the variability and uncertainty of grid carbon emissions, creating a need for user-side energy storage to support low-carbon regulation. Battery–ice hybrid energy storage systems combine rapid power response with intertemporal load shifting. However, dynamic carbon signals do not directly specify the required real-time regulation power or its allocation between battery and ice storage. Day-ahead–real-time signal deviations and heterogeneous operating constraints further complicate coordinated dispatch. This study proposes an optimization-guided residual reinforcement learning method for real-time low-carbon dispatch. A unified equivalent-power model is developed, and a day-ahead mixed-integer linear programming model uses the dynamic carbon emission responsibility factor of electricity (Cr) to generate low-carbon power and state-of-charge reference trajectories. An online feasible baseline is constructed from real-time device states, and a residual soft actor–critic policy incrementally corrects the references according to real-time Cr deviations. A case study at Hangzhou Medicine Port demonstrates robust performance across different Cr-deviation patterns. Compared with day-ahead optimization, the method reduces seven-day cumulative carbon emission responsibility by 8.54% and improves the low-carbon demand matching degree from −0.63 to −0.71. Post-hoc economic evaluation shows a 3.42% increase in operating revenue. Ablation results show that optimization guidance achieved 339.8% and 42.3% greater reductions in carbon emission responsibility relative to the final reductions achieved with rule guidance and no guidance, respectively. The proposed method enables heterogeneous user-side electrical and thermal storage to provide real-time low-carbon grid response.
keywords: dynamic carbon emission responsibility factor of electricity (Cr)

title: Hybrid WRF-ML modeling for characterizing inter- and intra-LCZ microclimate variability: A case study of Shenzhen, China
abstract: Understanding microclimatic variations across Local Climate Zones (LCZs) is crucial for optimizing urban morphology to enhance human thermal comfort and promote sustainable urban environments. While numerous studies have examined the spatio-temporal patterns and underlying mechanisms of thermal environments in different LCZ types, temperature variability within identical LCZs remain insufficiently explored. Moreover, research on other microclimate factors—such as relative humidity (RH) and wind speed (WS)—at both inter- and intra-LCZ scales is limited. In this study, a hybrid modeling framework based on the Weather Research and Forecast (WRF) model was proposed to accurately predict near-surface meteorological fields. It was achieved by refining the Urban Canopy Model (UCM) during the preprocessing stage of the WRF model and then integrating ML algorithms during its postprocessing stage. The predictive performance of four WRF-based datasets was evaluated and compared under relatively stable weather conditions across four seasons. The best-performing ML(XGBoost)-enhanced model dataset was applied to identify multivariate microclimate variations both inter- and intra-LCZs. The analysis was conducted in Shenzhen, a coastal hilly city in southern China. The results revealed that: (1) the WRF-ML hybrid models performed significantly better than the Standard and UCM-refined WRF models, with the optimal XGBoost-enhanced model achieving hourly average RMSE values of 0.613 K for AT, 1.131 % for RH, and 0.207 m/s for WS; (2) unique local geographic conditions, such as coastal surroundings and continuous natural landscapes, significantly influence microclimate variations within urban built-up areas; (3) inter-LCZ microclimate differences were generally within 1.5 K for AT, 9 % for RH, and 0.7 m/s for WS, exceeding intra-LCZ differences; and (4) built-up LCZs could be further divided into 2∼4 subcategories with distinct microclimate conditions, some of which showed relatively favorable microclimate environments during the high temperature period.

title: Addressing synergistic climate-urbanization impacts: A coupled PLUS-ML framework for projecting future LCZ and SUHI
abstract: Studies have assessed the individual effects of global warming and urbanization on urban thermal stress, yet the synergistic effects of global warming interacting with both urban expansion and intensification in the urbanization process on surface urban heat island (SUHI) have not been clarified. To analyze these synergy effects, we propose an integrated predictive framework that couples an improved PLUS model for Local Climate Zone (LCZ) transitions and a machine learning-based land surface temperature (LST) prediction module incorporating the global warming signal. Applied to the Wuhan Metropolitan Area (WMA), the proposed framework simulated LCZ and LST patterns from 2020 to 2030 under five scenarios. Utilizing the summer mean LST, near-surface air temperature, and LCZ maps from 2005 to 2020 as training data, the prediction model achieved an R² of 0.82 and RMSE of 0.70 °C. The contributions of urbanization and global warming to the increase of LST from 2020 to 2030 in the Natural Growth Scenario (NGS) are found to be 3.93 °C and 1.59 °C, respectively. The scenario analysis on the spatial variations on the SUHI changes via LCZ reveals that the environmental protection scenario (EPS) associated with the lowest SUHI increase, while the urban development scenario (UDS) corresponds to the highest warming with the spatial-average LST rising up to 0.82 °C in urban LCZ. Targeted strategies are then proposed to alleviate thermal risks and enhance climate resilience in the WMA. This study provides a scientific foundation for designing sustainable urban interventions and climate-resilient development policies amid compound environmental challenges.

title: Towards scenario-conditioned urban renewal using a progressive CP-GAN framework under heat–carbon–wind scenarios
abstract: High-density cities face escalating challenges from heat stress, carbon emissions, and reduced airflow. However, optimizing three-dimensional morphologies for urban renewal has been constrained by data complexity and computational bottlenecks, preventing real-time application. To address this gap, this study proposed a progressive conditional generative framework (CP-GAN) that integrated Pix2Pix and CycleGAN to synthesize urban forms conditioned on Local Climate Zones (LCZs) and to evaluate their responses to cooling and carbon-reduction objectives under prescribed near-surface wind conditions. The framework integrated multimodal inputs, including land surface temperature, carbon-emission intensity, and wind speed, with outputs capturing building morphology, land cover, and LCZ classification. The results showed that: (1) CP-GAN outperformed the Pix2Pix baseline, achieving an average SSIM of 0.835 and an R² of 0.792, with lower MSE and competitive PSNR; (2) Cooling-oriented optimization drove marked morphological shifts, reducing Floor Area Ratio (FAR) and Building Height (BH) by 37.6% and 25.9% on average, whereas carbon-focused optimization produced only moderate adjustments; (3) Green Ratio (GR) was a key driver of cooling optimization, increasing by 49.1% on average, but contributed little to carbon reduction, where FAR and BH played a dominant role; (4) Three scenario-conditioned pathways were identified: high-density blocks optimized through reductions in FAR and BH, medium-density blocks through enhanced green continuity and ventilation corridors, and inherently low-carbon parcels through incremental local adjustments. This study demonstrated how CP-GAN framework enables adaptive three-dimensional urban renewal by dynamically balancing heat mitigation, carbon reduction, and wind performance, thus providing a robust pathway for advancing climate-responsive design.

title: A multi-stage ROM-enhanced CFD-ML framework for efficient 3D urban wind-field prediction
abstract: Rapid assessment of urban wind environments is essential for early-stage sustainable and low-carbon urban design, yet conventional CFD becomes computationally prohibitive when multiple inflow directions and velocities are required. This study proposes a multi-stage ROM-enhanced CFD–ML framework for efficient and physically consistent urban wind-field prediction. A baseline CFD database is constructed using steady RANS simulations with sufficient surrounding-building layers. A reduced-order modeling (ROM) strategy coupled with machine learning reconstructs high-fidelity wind fields at unsampled velocities using a subset of inflow velocities, achieving R² ≥ 0.99 and reducing required CFD cases by at least 40% (e.g., 6 instead of 10 per direction); for two validation urban configurations, this yields savings of approximately 112 h of CFD computation time. Using the ROM-enhanced database, a morphology-driven surrogate is trained with eight urban morphological parameters plus inflow conditions to predict u, v, and w. The best MLP and XGBoost models reach R² > 0.99 for u and v and R² > 0.98 for w, while XGBoost trains markedly faster and is selected. Without additional CFD-based learning on unseen cases, the model delivers high-accuracy 3D wind-field predictions under oblique inflow and different urban layouts, achieving normalized percentage errors below 5% at pedestrian height, while quantitative profile-based metrics confirm preservation of height-dependent flow structures from pedestrian level to rooftop. Compared with conventional CFD, the trained ML model achieves approximately two orders of magnitude computational speedup. SHAP-based interpretability analysis confirms physically meaningful morphology-wind relationships. Overall, the framework offers an efficient, scalable, and interpretable solution for rapid 3D urban wind assessment in early-stage design and urban climate studies.

title: Reconstruction of fine-scale turbulence using GAN- and diffusion-based super-resolution models for Urban Air Mobility applications
abstract: This study evaluated deep-learning-based super-resolution (SR) models at an extreme 20× scaling factor using the Parallelized Large-Eddy Simulation Model (PALM) over a real urban environment. Such an evaluation addresses the practical need for fine-scale turbulent flows in complex urban environments relevant to Urban Air Mobility (UAM) applications. To investigate SR strategies, we employed two models: the Enhanced Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Network (ESRGAN), which directly performs 20× scaling, and a pretrained Latent Diffusion Model (LDM), trained on natural images, which uses a fixed 4× network with interpolation to achieve an overall resolution increase from 100 m to 5 m. The experiments provide a comparative assessment of GAN- and diffusion-based models for reconstructing fine-scale wind components (u, v, and w). The analysis evaluates not only visual reconstruction quality but also the physical consistency of the reconstructed fields, including the preservation of flow structures and energy spectra. ESRGAN effectively reconstructed fine-scale turbulent structures with good agreement in statistical metrics, whereas the pretrained LDM produced smoother reconstructions that preserved large-scale flow features. One-dimensional power spectral density analysis revealed that both models aligned well with the HR reference in the intermediate-to-high wavenumber range. However, at the highest wavenumbers, ESRGAN exhibited irregular spectral fluctuations, while the LDM showed a more rapid energy decay. Notably, both models demonstrated closer agreement with HR under stronger turbulence conditions. The proposed framework enables near real-time 3D turbulent field reconstruction, highlighting its potential for practical UAM applications.

title: Spatiotemporal dynamics and multidimensional drivers of urban diurnal temperature range: Evidence from integrated learning at the national scale in China
abstract: Urbanization and global warming are profoundly altering the diurnal temperature range (DTR), a key indicator of climate change with direct implications for public health and urban resilience. Yet, systematic evidence disentangling DTR dynamics across climatic zones at the national scale remains scarce. Using 1 km resolution MODIS LST data for China (2010–2020), this study integrates spatiotemporal trend analysis with explainable machine learning to characterize national DTR patterns and identify their heterogeneous drivers. The results show that: (1) daytime surface warming (+0.013 °C yr⁻¹) has outpaced nighttime warming (+0.008 °C yr⁻¹), leading to an overall slight increase in DTR, with the trend most pronounced in the warm temperate zone; (2) natural systems exert the strongest influence (42.1 %), with proximity to water bodies acting as the most critical regulator—reducing DTR by 2–3 °C within 5 km—while vegetation effects are strongly climate-dependent; (3) urban physical morphology exerts dual impacts, as high built-up density generally amplifies DTR, whereas taller buildings mitigate it by enhancing ventilation; and (4) socioeconomic factors overall moderate DTR, with population density showing the most consistent effect, while nighttime light intensity anomalously amplifies DTR in humid regions. By systematically revealing the climatic heterogeneity of DTR drivers, this study underscores the pivotal role of water bodies and urban form in regulating urban heat. The findings provide a scientific basis for context-specific nature-based solutions and resilience-oriented planning strategies to mitigate thermal risks under accelerating climate change and urbanization.
